impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not apply under AIA § 102(d)(2) to determine a reference patent's prior art date—is correct, or whether a reference patent can only claim its provisional application's filing date if at least one claim is supported by the provisional's written description.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's final written decision finding Dental Monitoring's patent claims obvious and remanded for reconsideration. The court addressed the critical question of how to determine the effective prior art date of a reference patent under AIA § 102(d)(2) when that patent claims priority to a provisional application. This ruling has significant implications for IPR proceedings and patent validity challenges relying on prior art references with provisional priority claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially narrower framework for establishing prior art dates of reference patents in IPR proceedings, making it harder for petitioners to use reference patents as prior art based solely on provisional filing dates without adequate written description support.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patent validity in IPR proceedings may face additional hurdles in establishing that reference patents qualify as prior art under AIA § 102(d)(2), potentially weakening their ability to invalidate competitors' patents.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement for method claims directed to administering a genus of antibodies for treating headache permits broad functional genus claims where any member of the genus would be effective, or whether such claims are invalid for lack of enablement under Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing on the enablement standard for method claims involving a genus of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement for method claims and undermines medical innovation by sustaining overly broad claims. The case has major implications for pharmaceutical and biotech patent claiming strategies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from the panel decision's approach, which may allow broader method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of biological molecules where any member of the genus would be therapeutically effective.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar companies face potentially broader patent claims blocking market entry, and the dissent signals ongoing uncertainty about the scope of enablement for functional genus claims in the life sciences.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether the agreement automatically terminated when the licensee shifted its business operations to patent enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue without joining A&M. The court also held the agreement did not terminate when TexasLDPC shifted to enforcement activities. This decision clarifies when an exclusive license is tantamount to an assignment for standing purposes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clearer standards confirming that exclusive licenses conveying all substantial rights allow suit without joining the patent owner, and that shifting to enforcement activities does not necessarily terminate a license agreement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on lack of standing or joinder requirements, and the ruling may facilitate patent enforcement by licensing entities that do not actively practice the patented technology.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether sufficient evidence supported Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two damages models it had previously rejected. The court reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract damages award and reinstated it, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation. This case provides significant guidance on trade secret damages methodologies and the scope of permissible expert testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from the court's instruction to consider additional damages models, potentially leading to larger recoveries, and from the reinstatement of the full jury award on breach of contract claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license or access third-party software face increased exposure for trade secret misappropriation claims, and the ruling may expand the range of admissible damages theories in trade secret litigation.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction involving functionality questions in design patents should be decided by a jury rather than the court.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing on design patent infringement standards under Egyptian Goddess, with significant concurrences and dissents. Chief Judge Moore dissented arguing the framework improperly allows summary judgment based on differences without adequate prior art consideration. The case highlights a deep split on the court regarding design patent infringement methodology and the role of juries in functionality determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Design patent defendants benefit from the current framework's allowance of summary judgment based on visual differences, providing earlier and less costly resolution of design patent disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a framework that multiple judges view as improperly focused on dissimilarities, potentially making it harder to prove infringement, particularly at summary judgment without prior art consideration.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems claim patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility for some patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement, and affirmed the damages award. The case provides important guidance on patent eligibility for communication technology standards-related patents and the boundary between abstract mathematical concepts and patent-eligible implementations in digital communication systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies holding patents on communication standards implementations benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility for certain claims tied to specific technical implementations, supporting patent enforcement in the standards-essential patent space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement liability, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the scope of patentable subject matter for optimization-based communication technologies.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a dispute over the interpretation of a settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of a patent reexamination necessarily raises a substantial patent law question sufficient for Federal Circuit jurisdiction, or is merely a state law contract dispute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a contract dispute about whether patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, finding the case was fundamentally about contract interpretation under state law rather than patent law. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for post-settlement patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that post-settlement contract disputes will be resolved under state law in regional circuits, potentially providing more predictable and party-favorable contract interpretation standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies may face uncertainty about which appellate court will review disputes arising from patent settlement agreements, and the ruling may complicate settlement drafting by requiring parties to consider both patent law and state contract law implications.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted patent claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching impedance for wireless transmission are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court had found them indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that the patent claims were not enabled because the specification did not adequately teach a person skilled in the art how to make and use the claimed invention. This case demonstrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on grounds not relied upon by the district court.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing additional pathways to invalidate asserted patents even when the district court's primary rationale is reversed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that claims surviving one invalidity challenge may still be invalidated on alternative grounds raised by defendants, increasing the unpredictability of patent litigation outcomes.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in denying leave to amend a patent infringement complaint, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal without leave to amend, the exceptional case fee award to Volkswagen, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found the proposed amended complaint was futile and upheld the finding that the case was exceptional under § 285. This decision reinforces consequences for pursuing weak patent infringement claims and provides guidance on attorney sanctions in patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from robust enforcement of fee-shifting under § 285 and attorney sanctions, deterring frivolous patent assertions and reducing litigation costs for accused infringers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened risk of fee awards and sanctions when pursuing infringement claims that courts deem insufficiently supported, potentially chilling legitimate but aggressive patent enforcement strategies.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court's order denying Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 must provide sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review, particularly where the plaintiff pursued infringement claims after the PTO rejected related claims under § 101 following Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and fees because the district court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful review. The case arose where the patent owner pursued infringement claims on a patent after the PTO had rejected claims in related applications under § 101, and the owner had abandoned those related applications without overcoming the rejections. This decision emphasizes judicial accountability in fee-shifting determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants seeking fee awards benefit from the requirement that district courts provide reasoned explanations for denying sanctions, increasing the likelihood that courts will engage substantively with exceptional case arguments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who pursue infringement after adverse PTO § 101 rejections in related applications face increased scrutiny and potential fee exposure, even if the asserted patent itself was not directly subject to those rejections.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such a deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day filing deadline for sunset review participation is a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority. The statute's silence on a participation deadline does not prohibit Commerce from establishing one by regulation. This decision preserves Commerce's procedural framework for antidumping duty sunset reviews.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from the preservation of Commerce's procedural framework, which facilitates timely and orderly sunset reviews that may result in continuation of antidumping duty orders protecting them from unfairly priced imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign producers face continued strict procedural deadlines in sunset reviews, and missing the 15-day window could result in revocation of antidumping duty orders without a full substantive review.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), particularly where the specification discloses both crystalline and amorphous forms of the salt.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of the malate salt patents have adequate written description. The decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent strategy because it upholds patent protection for specific crystalline salt forms of the cancer drug Cabometyx® (cabozantinib), which has substantial commercial value. The ruling reinforces that disclosure of both crystalline and amorphous forms can support claims to crystalline forms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies benefit from affirmation that written description requirements can be met for crystalline form patents through disclosure of preparation methods and characterization data, supporting protection of commercially valuable drug formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued patent barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, and the ruling may encourage broader claiming of crystalline pharmaceutical forms.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement action on both improper venue and patent eligibility (§ 101) grounds in the same order, or whether it must limit dismissal to the venue ground alone after finding venue improper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds. AML did not challenge the merits of either ruling but argued the court should have stopped after the venue dismissal. The decision confirms that district courts may reach the merits of patent eligibility even after finding venue is improper, providing defendants with potentially preclusive invalidity rulings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to obtain substantive patent eligibility rulings alongside venue dismissals, potentially precluding re-filing of the same claims in a proper venue and reducing serial litigation by patent assertion entities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders, particularly non-practicing entities, face the risk that a venue dismissal will be accompanied by a merits ruling on eligibility, potentially foreclosing the ability to refile in another district.
